Done. Here's what happened.

## Result

Orientation selectivity is demonstrated cleanly in **DANDI:000021** (Allen Institute Visual Coding, Neuropixels), using six sessions and 3,142 quality-controlled units. Among visually responsive cortical neurons, **73.6% have a significant orientation preference** on drifting gratings and 87.9% on static gratings, with a median tuning half-width of 37°. The same measurement on **hippocampal** units recorded on the same probes in the same sessions returns **6.2%**, essentially the 5% false-positive rate the permutation test is designed to produce. Visual thalamus sits in between at 36.6%, matching the classical picture of weak tuning in thalamic input that is sharpened in cortex.

A naive-Bayes decoder reading 128 cortical units identifies which of 8 grating directions was shown on a **single 2-second trial 72% of the time** (chance 12.5%), while the same decoder on hippocampal populations stays flat at chance. A neuron's preferred orientation is the same whether measured with 2 s drifting gratings or 0.25 s static gratings (median difference 15° against a chance value of 45°).

## Two real bugs I found and fixed

The directory already contained a partially-complete pipeline from an interrupted earlier session, so I audited it rather than trusting it. Two defects would have corrupted the conclusions:

**The cached response data was stale and misaligned.** `responses.pkl` was written at 10:22, but the loader was fixed at 10:23–10:24 to reorder unit metadata onto pynapple's sorted `TsGroup` ordering. The cached metadata rows therefore followed raw file order while the firing-rate matrix columns followed sorted order, so brain-area labels were scrambled across units. I re-ran extraction with the corrected loader and verified alignment across all six sessions.

**The GLM's pseudo-R² was meaningless.** The Poisson log-likelihood dropped the `log(k!)` term. That term cancels in a likelihood *difference* but not in McFadden's *ratio*, and without it the log-likelihood goes positive for any unit firing more than about one spike per trial. Medians were negative and values ranged from −36 to +88. With the term restored, the model comparison is orderly: 0.034 for temporal frequency alone, 0.169 for direction plus temporal frequency.

I also found and fixed a statistical circularity of my own diagnosis: responsiveness was being tested using each unit's *best* direction, which pre-selects for the very orientation contrast the selectivity test then measures. Pooling over all directions dropped the hippocampal false-positive rate from 17% to 6.2%.

## Honest caveats, stated in the outputs

Tuning widths are fit to only 8 directions spaced 45° apart, so widths below ~20° aren't resolvable; I added a rejection rule for fits that extrapolate a peak taller than anything measured (this moved the median from an implausible 26° to 37°). The hippocampal control is *not* clean for static gratings: 19% (13 of 69 units) rather than 5%. I tested block-shuffled and circular-shift nulls to see whether firing-rate nonstationarity explained it; neither did. The effect size is negligible regardless (median z of 0.24 versus 9.78 in cortex), so the regional contrast holds, but I did not paper over it.

## Deliverables in the working directory

`orientation_selectivity_dandi.py` (1,594-line jupytext script, self-contained, verified to run from a completely cleared cache and reproduce every number exactly), `orientation_selectivity_dandi.ipynb` (executed, 0 errors), nine `.png` figures, and `README.md`. Every figure was visually inspected and several were revised for label collisions, an overshooting fit, and a noisy population trace whose caption overstated what it showed.
